papers.title: Weighted pseudo-values for partly unobserved group membership in paediatric stem cell transplantation studies.
papers.one_line: Estimates long-term survival under transplantation against chemotherapy in childhood leukaemia by weighting pseudo-values for the probability that a donor would have been found, where the group a child belongs to is unknown if the search stopped early.
papers.what_was_done: Studies comparing allogeneic stem cell transplantation with chemotherapy in childhood leukaemia compare cohorts defined by whether a suitable donor was available, an approach that mimics genetic randomization. The difficulty is that donor availability becomes known only after the search completes: if a child relapses, dies or has another disease-specific event during the search, the indication for transplantation is lost, the search stops, and group membership remains unknown. The existing generalised pseudo-value approach treats donor identification as a binary time-dependent covariate and uses inverse probability of censoring weighting to adjust for non-identified donors, at the cost of repeated redefinitions of the risk set and an explicit waiting-time adjustment. This paper instead attaches weights to common pseudo-values reflecting the probability that a donor would have been identified had the search continued, so only a single risk set is needed and the weights depend on how much search time had elapsed, since a longer elapsed search makes identification less likely. Simulations show both approaches approximately unbiased with satisfactory confidence interval coverage in typical scenarios, with the weighted approach preferable where donor search takes much longer than usual, and 40 to over 90 times faster. In the worked leukaemia example the weighted approach shows that a faster search might have found up to 38 more donors while about 33 percent of patients have no donor available at all.

future_research.gap: Previously published transplantation studies analysed within the Cox framework may need reanalysis, since the treatment recommendations rest on those estimates.
future_research.quote: Previous SCT studies that have been analysed within the Cox model framework may be reanalysed with the new approach to reassess treatment effects and resulting treatment recommendations.

problems.evidence: The variable defining which arm a child belongs to, whether a matching donor exists, is a property of the world that exists independently of the child's survival, and it is observed only for those who survive long enough for the search to finish. That is an eligibility criterion whose value is unrecorded precisely for the people whose outcomes matter most, and the paper's response is to model the probability of what the unobserved value would have been.
problems.quote: It may happen that a patient suffers death, relapse, or other primary disease-specific problems during the donor search period. Consequently, the indication for SCT will be lost, donor search will be ceased, and donor availability status will remain unknown for this patient.

problems.evidence: Both approaches use donor identification rather than transplantation actually performed as the grouping variable, which is what avoids selection on surviving to the operation, and the weighted version handles the unobserved cases by a probability that decreases with elapsed search time. The result is a comparison of two strategies where the feasibility of one emerges over time, under non-proportional hazards, without a landmark and without discarding the early events.
problems.quote: Therefore, in order to avoid selection bias, it is crucial that statistical approaches consider donor identification rather than SCT applied.

problems.evidence: The existing approach requires repeated rounds of computation with different starting times and different risk sets, and the alternative needs only common pseudo-values computed once, running between 40 and more than 90 times faster in the simulation scenarios. The gap widens as more donors are identified, so the computational cost of the earlier method rises exactly with the amount of data available.
problems.quote: In the considered simulation scenarios of Section D of Supplemental Materials , the median WPV runtime was at least 40 times to more than 90 times faster than the corresponding median GPV runtime (see Figure S14 in Section E of Supplemental Materials ).

papers.title: Survival analyses in cardiovascular research, part II: statistical methods in challenging situations.
papers.one_line: Educational review of survival methods for harder cardiovascular settings, covering stratified and frailty Cox models, immortal time from poorly assessed time-dependent variables, competing risks, multistate and recurrent-event models, and alternatives with weaker assumptions.
papers.what_was_done: The second of two educational articles introduces the methods needed once the basic survival toolkit runs out. Stratified Cox models and frailty models are presented for departures from proportional hazards and for unobserved heterogeneity, and immortal time bias is illustrated as arising from a poor assessment of time-dependent variables. The problem of multiplicity of outcomes, where a composite endpoint analyzed as time to first event is not optimal, is addressed through competing risks methods, multistate models and recurrent-event methods. Alternatives with less restrictive assumptions are then covered: the win ratio, restricted mean survival time and the accelerated failure time model. Each method is illustrated with examples from published cardiovascular research and discussed with its main strengths and limitations. The review states plainly that modeling survival data adequately is not a straightforward exercise and offers practical advice on what to consider before choosing a model and on how to interpret findings from the more complex approaches.

problems.evidence: A single educational review needs eight distinct model families to cover the situations a cardiovascular survival analysis actually meets, each carrying its own assumptions and its own interpretation, and it closes by stating that choosing among them is not straightforward. The reader is left with advice on what to consider rather than a rule, and the choice determines both the estimand and the assumption burden.
problems.quote:
Modelling adequately survival data is not a straightforward exercise. This review
has offered practical advice on what should be considered before choosing the most appropriate
model for survival data, as well as how to interpret the findings yielded by more complex
statistical approaches.

problems.evidence: The review locates immortal time bias not in a design decision but in how time-dependent variables are assessed, which places it inside the modeling step where a cardiovascular researcher is least likely to look for a design flaw. It is taught alongside stratified and frailty models as one of the technical complications of the Cox framework rather than as a question about when follow-up should begin.
problems.quote:
Here, we introduce stratified Cox models
and frailty models, as well as the immortal time bias arising from a poor assessment of timedependent variables.

papers.title: Pharmacoepidemiology for nephrologists (part 2): potential biases and how to overcome them.
papers.one_line: Review pairing each bias in routinely collected pharmacoepidemiologic data with a remedy, including the E-value, negative control outcomes and control cohorts for unmeasured confounding, and landmarking, time-varying exposure or cloning with censoring and weighting for immortal time.
papers.what_was_done: The review is written to let nephrologists appraise or conduct observational drug studies, and organizes itself around biases and their remedies. For confounding by indication it describes designs such as the active comparator, and for the residual it names three devices for investigating unmeasured confounding: the E-value, negative control outcomes and control cohorts. For prevalent user and immortal time biases it prescribes restriction to incident users and then one of three analytic routes, landmarking, a time-varying exposure, or the cloning, censoring and weighting method. Missing data and misclassification are covered briefly. The conclusion draws a line between what design can prevent and what has to be quantified afterward: researchers can and should prevent immortal time and prevalent user biases in the design, confounding by indication is tackled by an active comparator with adequate adjustment, and where concerns about confounding or misclassification remain, quantifying their impact on the effect estimates is recommended.

problems.evidence: The registry entry says negative controls, proxies and validation data are not integrated into a standard workflow. This review does integrate three devices into a review aimed at practitioners, naming the E-value, negative control outcomes and control cohorts as the tools for investigating unmeasured confounding alongside the design that limits it. What it supplies is a menu with a recommendation to quantify when concerns remain, not a procedure connecting what a negative control shows to what the estimate should become.
problems.quote: We first describe designs to handle confounding by indication (e.g. active comparator design) and methods to investigate the influence of unmeasured confounding, such as the E-value, the use of negative control outcomes and control cohorts.

problems.evidence: The review separates the timing biases from the confounding ones by what can be done about them: immortal time and prevalent user bias are stated to be preventable in the design and therefore the researcher's responsibility to prevent, while confounding is something to be tackled and then quantified. Three analytic routes are given without a rule for choosing among them, and they target different estimands.
problems.quote: Researchers can and should prevent problems arising from immortal time and prevalent-user biases in their study design.

papers.title: Warning of Immortal Time Bias When Studying Drug Safety in Pregnancy: Application to Late Use of Antibiotics and Preterm Delivery.
papers.one_line: Shows in 549,082 Lombardy deliveries that treating third-trimester antibiotic use as a time-fixed exposure gives a null hazard ratio of 0.96 while the time-varying analysis gives 1.27, reversing the direction of the association.
papers.what_was_done: Antibiotics in late pregnancy are prescribed as therapy, so their use is a proxy for infection, which is a major cause of preterm birth, and an increased risk among treated women is therefore expected. A population-based cohort of 549,082 deliveries in Lombardy between 2007 and 2017, with 23,638 premature deliveries at 4.3 percent, was analyzed twice. Treating third-trimester antibiotic dispensing as a time-fixed exposure gave an adjusted hazard ratio for preterm delivery of 0.96 with an interval of 0.92 to 1.01, that is, no association or a hint of protection. Treating it as time-varying gave 1.27 with an interval of 1.21 to 1.34, and the same pattern held for low birth weight and low Apgar score. The mechanism is set out plainly: a woman is classified as exposed at a prescription date, and had a preterm birth occurred before that date she would have been classified unexposed, so the interval from the start of the third trimester to the first prescription is immortal and misclassified as exposed time. The paper notes that a conventional cohort comparison of users against non-users systematically produces an unexpected independence or apparent protection, which is strange given what antibiotic use marks. Remaining limitations include the delay between infection onset and dispensing and over-the-counter antibiotics, both diluting toward the null.

future_research.gap: Drugs associated with reduced preterm delivery, progesterone, tocolytics and antenatal steroids, are not recorded and were not accounted for, so the causal model of preterm birth remains incompletely specified.
future_research.quote: Therefore, because some drugs associated with reduced preterm delivery rates (e.g., progesterone, tocolytic drugs, and antenatal steroids) were not taken into account in our study, further investigations are needed to better understand the causal model of preterm birth and its correlates.

problems.evidence: The correction does not shrink an inflated estimate; it reverses the sign. A time-fixed analysis of half a million deliveries gives a null or faintly protective association where the substantive expectation is harm, and allocating the pre-prescription person-time correctly gives a 27 percent increase. The paper notes this pattern is systematic in conventional cohort comparisons of this kind, so the direction of a published finding in this literature is a function of the exposure definition.
problems.quote: The present study showed how incorrect allocation of exposure person-time may strongly affect and even reverse the direction of the investigated association.

problems.evidence: The exposure is a dispensing record standing in for infection onset, and the paper identifies two distinct error sources that both pull toward the null: the delay between the infection starting and the drug being dispensed misclassifies person-weeks as unexposed to infection, and antibiotics obtained over the counter are absent from the database entirely. Neither is propagated into the estimate, and both work against the finding the paper reports.
problems.quote: Rather, the delay between infection onset and the date of drug dispensing could lead to misclassification of a certain number of person-weeks as currently exposed to infection, thus diluting the point estimates toward the null.

papers.title: Analysis of time-to-event for observational studies: Guidance to the use of intensity models.
papers.one_line: STRATOS guidance on hazard models for observational time-to-event data, with checklists for fitting, assessing and interpreting them, and an explicit statement that causal conclusions from such models are difficult to draw.
papers.what_was_done: This guidance covers the conduct of time-to-event analysis in observational studies through intensity models, beginning with the time axis, event definition and censoring, then hazard models with emphasis on Cox regression. Checklists are supplied for fitting the model, assessing goodness of fit and interpreting results, with attention to avoiding immortal time bias by introducing time-dependent covariates. It works through practical difficulties: partial likelihood needs the time-dependent covariate value for everyone at risk at every event time, so extrapolation is often needed and last value carried forward is the usual device, which biases toward the null when the hazard truly depends on the current unknown value. Covariates changing shortly before the endpoint are flagged as particularly suspicious, with medication changes in the final weeks before death as the example, and the most serious case identified as reverse causality where the covariate changes because of early symptoms of the event. Joint longitudinal-survival models are noted as a more advanced route that also allows measurement error. The summary states that the most important item in planning is to specify the research question clearly and consider whether the data can answer it, and identifies risk prediction for non-fatal events and causal inference as questions for which an intensity model is only one step.

future_research.gap: An intensity model is only a partial answer for causal inference and for prediction of non-fatal events, and further analyses are needed.
future_research.quote:
We have also
identified research questions for which an intensity model only provides one step towards an answer and where further analyses
are needed. These include risk prediction for non-fatal events and causal inference.

future_research.gap: Competing risks, recurrent events, general multistate models, accelerated failure time and additive hazards models, frailty and joint models, relative survival and interval censoring are all left out.
future_research.quote: Even though the paper is not short, it fails to discuss a number of aspects that are also of importance.

problems.evidence: A time-dependent covariate is needed for everyone at risk at every event time and is measured only when someone happened to record it, so the analysis carries the last value forward. The guidance states this biases toward the null when the hazard depends on the current unknown value, and identifies the worse case: a covariate that changes because early symptoms of the event have appeared, which makes the observation process a consequence of the outcome.
problems.quote: However, such lastvalue-carried-forward approach can induce some bias toward the null if the current hazard depends truly on the current (unknown) covariate value 23,24 .

problems.evidence: Guidance written by a large group of biostatisticians for the analysis of observational time-to-event data names, as one of its own topics, the difficulties in drawing proper causal conclusions from hazard models. The model that dominates this literature, with more than thirty thousand citations by the paper's own count, is therefore presented as one whose output does not straightforwardly correspond to a causal quantity.
problems.quote:
We discuss prediction based on hazard
models and difficulties when attempting to draw proper causal conclusions from such
models.

problems.evidence: The guidance supplies checklists that place immortal time alongside the specification of the time axis, delayed entry and the handling of time-dependent covariates, so the timing decisions are made explicit items to be worked through rather than left implicit. It states firmly that the checklists are not cook books and that the most important step is specifying the question and asking whether the data can answer it, which leaves the timing choices as judgments to be documented.
problems.quote:
We have provided some checklists that we find useful to consider, however, it is important to emphasize that these checklists
cannot be taken as ‘cook books’ on how to conduct time to event analysis in observational studies.

papers.title: Statistical Analysis of Clinical COVID-19 Data: A Concise Overview of Lessons Learned, Common Errors and How to Avoid Them.
papers.one_line: Sets out why in-hospital COVID-19 data, bounded by admission and discharge, invite competing risk and immortal time errors, and states that the authors regard many published in-hospital treatment results as untrustworthy.
papers.what_was_done: In-hospital data are restricted by definition to the interval between admission and discharge alive or dead, and the paper argues this restriction carries a substantial risk that inappropriate methods are used. It works through the common errors with clinical examples drawn mostly from other infections. Kaplan-Meier plots are widely used for time-dependent events such as intensive care admission, invasive ventilation or hospital death when only hospital data are available, which censors patients discharged without the event; the paper states this is not a meaningful model assumption because discharged patients are in better health than those still hospitalized, and that cumulative incidence functions should be used instead. It also covers errors arising with time-dependent covariates and with conditioning on future events. The discussion notes that these issues have been known for years, explained by formulae, simulation and real analyses, and that most bias-reducing methods are easy to apply in standard software, yet have not been widely adopted. It attributes part of the problem to the compression of peer review under the rush to publish, and states the authors' concern that many current results on in-hospital treatment of COVID-19 patients are untrustworthy.

future_research.gap: Better-suited statistical methods exist and are implemented in standard software but have not been adopted, so the gap is uptake rather than availability.
future_research.quote: statistical methods that are better suited to these data have yet to be widely adopted

problems.evidence: Censoring at discharge is the default in these analyses and is stated to be not a meaningful assumption, because discharge is informative: discharged patients are healthier than those who remain. The competing event is therefore removed as data cleaning in the standard plot used to present these results, and the paper's remedy is to replace the plot with cumulative incidence functions rather than to justify the censoring.
problems.quote: However, this implies that patients discharged without the event are censored. This is not a meaningful model assumption, since discharged patients are usually in a better health condition than hospitalized patients.
problems.locator: Inappropriate Use of Kaplan-Meier Survival Plots

problems.evidence: The authors state that they regard many published results on in-hospital treatment as untrustworthy, and attribute this partly to reduced time for detailed peer review. The judgment is available to them because the errors are structural and visible from the methods, which means nothing in the reporting or review process was carrying that check, and their proposed remedy is greater involvement of statisticians rather than any requirement on what a study must report.
problems.quote: We are concerned that many current results that examine the in-hospital treatment of COVID-19 patients are untrustworthy.

papers.title: Immortal time bias: a possible explanation for "Impact of acyclovir use on survival of patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia and high load herpes simplex virus replication".
papers.one_line: Letter identifying two distinct routes by which immortal time could produce the reported dramatic mortality reduction from antiviral treatment, depending on whether treatment preceded or followed the diagnostic test.
papers.what_was_done: A study had reported that acyclovir dramatically reduces mortality in ventilator-associated pneumonia with high herpes simplex virus load. The letter accepts the question as important and objects to the survival analysis, which separates patients into treated and untreated. It notes that immortal time bias substantially overestimates treatment effects and that even a treatment with no effect can produce large statistically significant estimates under it. Two scenarios are then set out, both of which favour the treated group. If acyclovir treatment precedes the positive test and time starts at treatment, the interval from treatment to test is immortal time inside the treated group. If the positive test precedes treatment, the interval is excluded from the untreated group. The remedy proposed is to start observation at the date of the herpes simplex virus test and to include acyclovir as a time-updated exposure.

problems.evidence: The letter shows that the same comparison can be biased in the same direction through two different mechanisms depending on the order of two events, treatment and diagnostic test, neither of which the reader can determine from the published report. It also states the general property that makes the bias hard to detect from results alone: a treatment with no effect can produce large and significant estimates.
problems.quote: Even for medical treatment without effect, that bias may lead to large estimates that are “statistically significant”.

papers.title: Learning from registries in pulmonary arterial hypertension: pitfalls and recommendations.
papers.one_line: Reviews what registries have contributed to knowledge of pulmonary arterial hypertension and discusses the methodological conditions on that contribution, including immortal time bias, data quality and the effect of new data protection rules on harmonisation.
papers.what_was_done: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is rare and incurable, and registries collecting observational data have supplied what trials in selected populations cannot: incidence and prevalence across subgroups, rising age at presentation, stagnating diagnostic delay, the importance of haemodynamic definition criteria and of cardiac comorbidities. The review traces the transformation of therapeutic management, the still insufficient use of combination therapy, the improvement in outcome, emerging evidence against anticoagulation, and the validity of risk-stratification tools derived from large registries. It then turns to methodology, discussing immortal time bias, registry data quality and the recommendations of European organisations. The section on data governance notes that the General Data Protection Regulation adopted in 2016 could hamper collection of medical data by requiring specific consent at every use, that member states can set their own research exemptions so the rules may differ across countries, and that this endangers the sharing of data and slows research. The conclusion calls for registry methodology to conform to current recommendations and for harmonisation of data collection and reuse of data to be prioritised.

future_research.gap: Interoperability of patient registries remains incomplete and a number of complex challenges are unaddressed.
future_research.quote: These initiatives are a first step towards greater interoperability of patient registries, although a number of complex challenges remain to be addressed.

problems.evidence: The review's closing priorities are harmonisation of data collection and reuse of data, which are stated as goals rather than achievements for a disease whose evidence base is built from registries at local, regional, national and international level. The governance section adds a specific obstacle: research exemptions under the data protection regulation are set nationally, so the rules governing what may be shared differ between countries pooling into the same analyses.
problems.quote: Finally, the harmonisation of data collections and the reuse of data should be prioritised.

problems.evidence: Immortal time bias appears in this review as one of the methodological aspects that condition what registry evidence can support, alongside data quality, in a field whose treatment recommendations, risk-stratification tools and evidence against anticoagulation all rest on registry analyses. Naming it among the pitfalls in a review of this kind means the estimates it discusses are not separated into those that handled it and those that did not.
problems.quote: Finally, the benefits of registries and methodological aspects are discussed, including immortal time bias, registry data quality and recommendations from EU organisations (EUCERD and PARENT).

papers.title: New-onset atrial fibrillation can be falsely associated with increased length of stay in ICU due to immortal time bias.
papers.one_line: Letter showing that an arrhythmia which can occur at any point during an intensive care stay will appear to lengthen that stay, and that the same structure can mask a real mortality increase as a null result.
papers.what_was_done: A study had reported that new-onset atrial fibrillation in critically ill adults was associated with longer intensive care and hospital stay and higher total costs, and that after adjustment there was no independent association with mortality. The letter argues both findings are shaped by immortal time. The arrhythmia can occur at any time during the stay, so patients who stay longer have more opportunity to develop it, and a patient developing it on day 4 could not have been discharged or died before day 4; those first three days are immortal because an outcome during them would have precluded the exposure. That time is attributed to the exposure without the exposure having contributed to it. The letter then makes the sharper point about the mortality result: the truth could be that the arrhythmia raises mortality, and the reported null could be the sum of a real adverse effect and a bias pointing the other way. Three remedies are proposed: restrict to patients with the arrhythmia on day 1, include it as a time-varying covariate in a Cox model, or use time-dependent propensity score matching on covariates influencing its onset.

problems.evidence: Where the exposure is an event that can occur at any time during follow-up and the outcome is the length of that follow-up, the two are linked by construction and a positive association is guaranteed. The letter's second point is more consequential: a null result after adjustment can be a real harmful effect cancelled by the bias, so correcting the timing can change a null into a signal rather than only shrinking an inflated one.
problems.quote: The truth could be that NOAF is associated with increased mortality risk, but since patients who lived longer can have more chances to experience NOAF, the neural effect reported in the paper was actually the result of the true adverse effect and the bias towards beneficial effect.

problems.evidence: The outcome under discussion is length of intensive care stay, which ends either in discharge or in death, so the two compete and a treatment or condition that raises early mortality shortens the stay. The letter notes that the same immortal time argument applies to the mortality outcome, and none of its three proposed remedies addresses the competing structure of discharge and death.
problems.quote: For example, a patient can have NOAF on day 4 and the outcome such as ICU discharge or death cannot happen before day 4.

papers.title: Methodological considerations when analysing and interpreting real-world data.
papers.one_line: Non-technical review of design elements for healthcare database studies, arguing that active-comparator new-user design controls confounding by design where analysis cannot, and noting that immortal time bias often cannot be distinguished from a real benefit.
papers.what_was_done: The review argues that where randomization is unavailable and the variables needed to address confounding analytically cannot be collected, design must do the work. The critical elements are new-user designs beginning follow-up at treatment initiation to reflect a hypothetical intervention with a clear timeline, active comparators contrasting alternatives for the same indication, and consideration of induction and latent periods, with propensity scores balancing measured covariates afterward. Immortal time bias is defined as arising when treatment is defined on a future event and the pre-initiation follow-up is classified as treated, which lowers the apparent rate in that group; it occurs particularly when treatments are given in sequence, such as biologic agents only after conventional ones, or when follow-up starts at different points in the treated and untreated groups. The review states that the bias is often strong enough to be detected because results look too good to be true, but that in many situations it cannot be distinguished from an expected benefit and can mask actual harm. The section on g-methods notes that confounding may be harder to control by weighting or g-estimation than by design, because data on the drivers of treatment change, lack of effectiveness and side effects, are often missing, and that doubly robust methods share this limitation.

future_research.gap: Machine learning could relax the parametric assumptions of the g-formula, but valid confidence intervals for causal estimands under machine learning remain a challenge.
future_research.quote: Current work on machine learning in causal inference is focused on enhancing the validity of confidence intervals for causal estimands, which remains a challenge [106].

problems.evidence: The review states that the bias is sometimes detectable because the result looks too good to be true, and then states the harder case: in many situations it is indistinguishable from a genuine treatment benefit, and it can conceal real harm. That removes the informal safeguard readers rely on, since only implausibly large estimates announce themselves and moderate ones do not.
problems.quote: In many situations, however, immortaltime bias cannot be distinguished from an expected treatment benefit and can mask actual harm.

problems.evidence: The review compares the estimator families on what they need rather than on how they perform: weighting and g-estimation model the treatment process, which requires data on why treatment changed, and lack of effectiveness and side effects are usually unrecorded; the g-formula models each time-varying confounder and the outcome and carries stronger modeling assumptions with several confounders; doubly robust methods also model treatment and so inherit the same limitation. The design-based alternative limits confounding without those models. Which to use therefore depends on what a database happens to record.
problems.quote: Compared with ACNU design, which limits unmeasured confounding by design, confounding bias may be more difficult to control using inverse-probability of treatment weights or g-estimation because we often have limited data on the drivers of treatment change (lack of effectiveness, side effects), which complicates modelling of the treatment process.

problems.evidence: The conclusion states that residual bias has to be evaluated carefully for each study, after design and analysis have both been applied, and offers no instrument for that evaluation. Treatment equipoise between the compared drugs is proposed as the property that makes an active comparator promising, judged by the absence of known strong predictors of either treatment, which is an argument about what is known rather than a measurement of what remains.
problems.quote:
Their impact on the potential for residual bias needs to
be carefully evaluated for each study.

papers.title: Resurrecting immortal-time bias in the study of readmissions.
papers.one_line: Compares two national readmission measures in 299,249 Medicare surgical patients and shows the measure counting 30 days from surgery rather than from discharge understates readmission by up to 36 percent relative, in proportion to length of stay.
papers.what_was_done: Two widely used definitions of 30-day readmission differ in their origin: the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services measure counts 30 days from discharge, and the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program measure counts 30 days from the index operation. Using a 20 percent sample of national Medicare data for 299,249 patients undergoing cystectomy, colectomy, abdominal aortic aneurysm repair and total knee arthroplasty between 2010 and 2014, with median lengths of stay of 9, 9, 3 and 4 days, the study computed readmission both ways. The ranking across procedures was the same under either measure, with cystectomy highest and knee arthroplasty lowest, but the absolute differences were 6.2, 3.7, 2.5 and 0.4 percentage points, corresponding to relative differences of 31, 36, 28 and 9 percent, with the surgery-anchored measure significantly lower for every procedure. The differences track length of stay. The paper explains that the bias attenuates the effect of readmission risk factors as length of stay rises, both by overlooking what happens during the inpatient stay and by shortening the window in which postdischarge exposures can act, and concludes that uniform outcome measures are needed and that reoperation or complication rate may be a better quality measure where stays are long or variable.

future_research.gap: Where length of stay is long or widely variable, readmission may be the wrong quality measure altogether and reoperation or complication rate may serve better.
future_research.quote: Reoperation rate or complication rate may be a more

problems.evidence: Two national measures of the same outcome differ only in where the 30-day window starts, and that difference alone changes the reported readmission rate by up to 36 percent in relative terms, with the gap proportional to length of stay. The bias also distorts the association with risk factors rather than only the level, since it shortens the window in which postdischarge exposures can act while ignoring the inpatient period.
problems.quote: bias increasingly attenuates the effect of these risk factors as length

problems.evidence: The two measures are properties of the data collection programmes rather than choices an analyst makes, and studies inherit whichever their data source implements. The paper's remedy is uniformity across measurement methodologies so that studies can be compared, which is a call for the sources to change rather than a check an investigator could apply before using one.
problems.quote:
Uniform outcome measures are needed to eliminate
ambiguity and synergize research and policy efforts.

papers.title: Bias in pharmacoepidemiologic studies using secondary health care databases: a scoping review.
papers.one_line: Reviews 117 articles on biases specific to secondary database pharmacoepidemiology, finding confounding raised in 63.2 percent, selection in 47.0 percent and measurement in 46.2 percent, with immortal time in 25.6 percent.
papers.what_was_done: An automated search of MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science for 2000 to 2018, supplemented by reference checking, identified 117 articles whose principal object was to highlight a bias in pharmacoepidemiologic studies using secondary databases, including essays, methodological reviews, simulations, letters and retractions. Publications on the limitations of these databases increased over time and across disciplines. Confounding was the most reported category at 63.2 percent, then selection at 47.0 percent and measurement at 46.2 percent, with confounding by indication at 32.5 percent, unmeasured or residual confounding at 28.2 percent, outcome misclassification at 28.2 percent and immortal time at 25.6 percent the commonest subcategories. The review collates remedies alongside the biases: restriction, matching and new-user designs at the design stage, stratification, regression, disease risk scores and propensity scores at the analysis stage, instrumental variables, proxies and external information for unmeasured confounding, g-estimation and marginal structural models for time-dependent confounding, and target trial emulation. It records where these fall short: control for unmeasured variables will never be optimal outside randomized crossover designs and even those remain subject to time-dependent confounding; protopathic bias is not confounding so adjustment is useless and only restriction or a lag time helps; and as-treated analyses censoring at discontinuation introduce informative censoring, mentioned in only 2.6 percent of articles.

future_research.gap: Frailty and healthy-user behaviour are strong determinants of outcome, are seldom measured in these databases, and are therefore very difficult to control.
future_research.quote: In observational studies of pharmacoepidemiologic databases, these types of behavior are seldom measured, thus making it very difficult to control for their effect [ 38 ].

problems.evidence: Unmeasured confounding is raised in more than a quarter of the 117 articles, and the review's own assessment of the remedies is that outside randomized crossover designs, control for unmeasured variables will never be optimal or, at best, one could never be sure that it is. That is the limit stated as a property of the design class rather than of any study, and even the exception it names remains open to time-dependent confounding.
problems.quote: At all events, with the exception of crossover designs, where the order in which a study participant receives the treatments is randomized, control for unmeasured variables will never be optimal or, at best, one could never be sure that it would be so.

problems.evidence: Outcome misclassification is among the four commonest subcategories at 28.2 percent, on a par with unmeasured confounding, and the review adds a structural point about confounder measurement: the databases were not designed for epidemiology, so data on over-the-counter drugs, frailty and smoking are absent or poor, which makes adjusting for them difficult or impossible rather than merely imprecise.
problems.quote: which renders it difficult or even impossible to adjust for such factors, in order to control for confounding

problems.evidence: The review introduces target trial emulation as the proposed approach and immediately qualifies it in the same sentence: the framework avoids common methodological pitfalls and leaves the adjustment for time-dependent confounders as the critical remaining problem. The pitfalls it prevents are the design-induced ones, and the identification problem is untouched, which is precisely the distinction the entry says gets collapsed.
problems.quote: Although the emulated target trial helps avoid common methodologic pitfalls, the appropriate adjustment for time-dependent confounders remains critical [ 34 ].

problems.evidence: An as-treated analysis censors patients who stop treatment, and those patients stop precisely because the expected clinical effect did not appear, so the censoring selects on the outcome. The review classifies this as a selection bias and reports that it is mentioned in 2.6 percent of the 117 articles it surveyed, so the mechanism most likely to affect a per-protocol analysis is among the least discussed.
problems.quote: In practice, this informative censoring (mentioned in only 2.6% of the articles reviewed, see Table 1 ) leads to a selection bias.
